message.content:
**Hydrogen – Key Physical & Chemical Properties**

| Property | Value / Description |
|----------|---------------------|
| **Atomic number** | 1 |
| **Symbol** | H |
| **Common isotopes** | ¹H (protium, ~99.98 %), ²H (deuterium, ~0.02 %) – stable; ³H (tritium) – radioactive (half‑life ≈12.32 y) |
| **Atomic mass** | 1.00794 u (average weighted by natural abundance) |
| **Electron configuration** | 1s¹ |
| **Electronegativity (Pauling)** | 2.20 |
| **First ionization energy** | 13.598 eV (1312 kJ mol⁻¹) |
| **Second ionization energy** | 27.211 eV (2625 kJ mol⁻¹) |
| **Electron affinity** | –72.8 kJ mol⁻¹ (negative, meaning it does *not* readily accept an extra electron) |
| **Molecular weight (H₂)** | 2.01588 g mol⁻¹ |
| **Boiling point (at 1 atm)** | –252.87 °C (20.44 K) |
| **Melting point (at 1 atm)** | –259.16 °C (14.01 K) |
| **Density at STP** | 0.08988 g L⁻¹ (≈0.0000899 kg m⁻³) |
| **Specific heat capacity (gas, 25 °C)** | 28.836 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹ (≈14.304 kJ kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) |
| **Heat of vaporization** | 0.449 kJ g⁻¹ (≈449 kJ kg⁻¹) |
| **Refractive index (visible light)** | 1.000132 (very close to vacuum) |
| **Solubility in water (25 °C)** | 7.9 g L⁻¹ (≈0.79 wt %) |
| **Flammability range in air** | 4–75 % (by volume) |
| **Bond dissociation energy (H–H)** | 436 kJ mol⁻¹ |
| **Dipole moment** | 0 D (nonpolar molecule) |
| **Spectral lines** | Lyman series (UV), Balmer series (visible) – classic “hydrogen spectrum” |
| **Typical uses** | Fuel cell technology, rocket propellant (liquid hydrogen), laboratory standard for spectroscopic calibration, medical imaging (MRI contrast agents using deuterated compounds), industrial processes (ethylene production, ammonia synthesis) |

---

### Quick Takeaways

- **Lightest element** – both atomically and molecularly; extremely low density.
- **Nonmetallic diatomic gas** – exists naturally as H₂ under normal conditions.
- **Highly reactive** – forms hydrides with many metals; reacts violently with oxygen (explosive).
- **Isotopic variants** – deuterium used in nuclear fusion research; tritium used in radiolabeling and fusion reactors.
- **Spectroscopically important** – hydrogen’s spectral lines were pivotal in developing quantum mechanics.

Feel free to ask if you’d like deeper details on any specific property or application!
